Description: explicit — validate style JSON with CLI tool after migration
prompt: I'm migrating from Mapbox to MapLibre and want to check whether my exported style JSON is compatible before deploying. Is there a CLI tool I can run on the file?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Thinking: We need to answer user: they want to check compatibility of exported style JSON before deploying, using a CLI tool. Provide info about maplibre-style-spec CLI, gl-style-validate, installation, usage, options, interpreting results, also mention Maputnik, style spec validation, maybe other tools. Provide steps. Also note version compatibility, handling of Mapbox-specific sources, etc. Provide example commands. Also mention that MapLibre style spec CLI can be installed via npm. Provide guidance on handling errors, customizing. Provide references. Ensure thorough answer. ## Quick answer Yes – the **MapLibre Style Specification CLI** can validate a style JSON against the MapLibre spec. ```bash # Install the validator (one‑time) npm i -g @maplibre/maplibre-style-spec # Run it on your exported style gl-style-validate path/to/style.json ``` If the command exits with `0` and prints **“✔︎ style is valid”**, the file conforms to the MapLibre style spec and can be loaded by `maplibre-gl`. Any warnings or errors will be listed with line/column numbers so you can fix them before you ship. Below is a complete walk‑through, plus extra tips for handling the few things that the validator can’t catch (e.g., Mapbox‑only source URLs, sprite/glyph locations, or custom extensions). --- ## 1. Install the validator The validator lives in the **`@maplibre/maplibre-style-spec`** package. You can install it globally (so the `gl-style-validate` command is on your `$PATH`) or locally to a project. | Option | Command | When to use | |--------|---------|-------------| | **Global** (recommended for a one‑off check) | `npm i -g @maplibre/maplibre-style-spec` | You want the command available from any folder. | | **Local (devDependency)** | `npm i -D @maplibre/maplibre-style-spec` | You want the tool version locked to your project’s `package.json`. Then run it with `npx gl-style-validate …`. | | **Yarn / pnpm** | `yarn global add @maplibre/maplibre-style-spec`
`pnpm add -g @maplibre/maplibre-style-spec` | Same as npm, just your preferred package manager. | > **Tip:** The CLI is bundled as an ES‑module. If you run it on a very old Node version (< 14) you’ll need to upgrade Node first. --- ## 2. Run the validator ```bash # Basic usage gl-style-validate my-style.json # Verbose output (shows every warning, not just errors) gl-style-validate -v my-style.json # Output as JSON (useful for CI pipelines) gl-style-validate -j my-style.json > validation-report.json ``` ### What you’ll see * **✅ ✔︎ style is valid** – no breaking issues. * **❌ Error** – a required property is missing or has the wrong type. The map will **fail to load** in MapLibre. * **⚠️ Warning** – the property is allowed but not part of the current MapLibre spec (e.g., a Mapbox‑only extension). The map will still load, but the feature may be ignored. Example output: ``` ❌ /sources/openstreetmap/type must be equal to one of the allowed values: vector, raster, geojson, image, video, canvas, model ⚠️ /layers/0/metadata/mapbox:group is not a recognized MapLibre property ✅ style is valid (1 warning, 0 errors) ``` In CI you can treat any non‑zero exit code as a failure: ```bash gl-style-validate my-style.json || exit 1 ``` --- ## 3. What the validator **does** & **doesn’t** check | ✅ Covered by `gl-style-validate` | ❌ Not covered (you must verify manually) | |-----------------------------------|-------------------------------------------| | JSON syntax & required fields (`version`, `sources`, `layers`, `glyphs`, `sprite`) | Whether the URLs you reference actually serve tiles, sprites, or glyphs (404s) | | Correct data types for every property (e.g., `paint` values, `layout` booleans) | Mapbox‑only source URLs (`mapbox://…`) – the validator will flag them as “unknown source type” but you still need to replace them with a real tile endpoint | | Presence of required top‑level keys (`center`, `zoom` are optional but validated if present) | Custom extensions (`metadata.mapbox:*`, `filter` expressions that use Mapbox‑only functions) | | Valid `sky` / `terrain` objects (MapLibre‑specific) | Whether the style’s sprite sheet actually contains the icons you reference (the validator only checks the JSON reference) | | Correct `source-layer` names for vector sources **if** the source definition is present in the same file (it can’t inspect remote tiles) | Runtime performance concerns (e.g., too many layers, huge source files) | **Bottom line:** The CLI guarantees that the JSON *conforms* to the spec; it can’t guarantee that the external resources exist or that Mapbox‑only extensions will be ignored gracefully. Those you’ll need to test by loading the style in a MapLibre map (or with a tool like **Maputnik**). --- ## 4. Typical migration fixes you’ll see When you export a style from Mapbox Studio, the validator will usually point out a handful of Mapbox‑specific items: | Issue | What the validator reports | How to fix it | |-------|----------------------------|---------------| | `type: "vector"` source with a `url: "mapbox://…"` | **Error** – unknown source type or URL scheme | Replace the URL with a public vector tile endpoint (e.g., `https://{s}.tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf` or your own PMTiles endpoint). Update `source-layer` names if they differ. | | `sprite: "mapbox://sprites/…"` | **Error** – sprite URL must be an HTTP(S) URL | Host the sprite sheet yourself (or use a free provider) and set `sprite: "https://my.cdn.com/sprites/sprite"` | | `glyphs: "mapbox://fonts/…"` | **Error** – glyph URL must be HTTP(S) | Use a public glyphs URL, e.g., `https://fonts.openmaptiles.org/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` | | `metadata.mapbox:group` or other `metadata.mapbox:*` keys | **Warning** – unknown property | Either delete the `metadata.mapbox:*` entries (they’re ignored by MapLibre) or rename them to something you control (`metadata.myapp:group`). | | `filter` expressions using `["==", ["get", "mapbox_id"], …]` | **Warning** – unknown property `mapbox_id` (if that property isn’t in your data) | Ensure the property exists in your source data, or replace the filter with a property you actually have. | | `setFog`‑related style properties (`fog`) | **Error** – `fog` is not a MapLibre style object | Convert to the `sky` object (see below). | ### Converting a Mapbox `fog` style to MapLibre `sky` ```json // Mapbox (invalid for MapLibre) { "fog": { "range": [0, 10], "color": "#f8f4f0", "high-color": "#ffffff", "space-color": "#c0d8ff", "horizon-blend": 0.3 } } ``` ```json // MapLibre equivalent { "sky": { "sky-type": "atmosphere", "sky-color": "#c0d8ff", "horizon-color": "#f8f4f0", "fog-color": "#ffffff", "sky-horizon-blend": 0.3, "atmosphere-blend": 0.5 } } ``` After you edit the JSON, run `gl-style-validate` again to confirm the error is gone. --- ## 5. Using the validator in a CI/CD pipeline If you have a build step that publishes styles (e.g., after a CI‑run of Maputnik), you can automatically block a deploy when the style is invalid. **GitHub Actions example** ```yaml name: Validate MapLibre style on: push: paths: - 'styles/**/*.json' jobs: style-check: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Install validator run: npm i -g @maplibre/maplibre-style-spec - name: Validate all styles run: | for f in styles/**/*.json; do echo "🔎 Validating $f" gl-style-validate -v "$f" done ``` If any style fails, the job exits with a non‑zero status and the PR cannot be merged. --- ## 6. Visual debugging with Maputnik (optional but handy) The CLI tells you *what* is wrong; **Maputnik** shows you *where* in the map it manifests. ```bash npm i -g maputnik maputnik path/to/style.json ``` * The UI will highlight any property that the validator flagged. * You can edit the style live, save, and re‑run the validator in one click. Maputnik also lets you **replace** Mapbox source URLs with your own tile endpoints via the UI, which can be faster than editing raw JSON. --- ## 7. Full example workflow ```bash # 1️⃣ Install tools (once) npm i -g @maplibre/maplibre-style-spec maputnik # 2️⃣ Export your style from Mapbox Studio → style.json # 3️⃣ Run the validator gl-style-validate -v style.json # → Fix any errors reported (replace mapbox:// URLs, add sprite/glyph URLs, convert fog → sky) # 4️⃣ (Optional) Open in Maputnik for visual tweaks maputnik style.json # edit → save → re‑run validator # 5️⃣ When clean, commit the final JSON git add style.json git commit -m "✅ Updated style for MapLibre" # 6️⃣ Deploy – the map will now load with # new maplibregl.Map({ style: '/path/to/style.json', ... }) ``` --- ## 8. Frequently asked follow‑up questions | Question | Answer | |----------|--------| | **Can I validate a style that references remote sources?** | The validator only checks the *structure* of the JSON. It does not fetch the remote tiles, sprites, or glyphs. After validation, load the style in a test page (or Maputnik) to confirm the URLs are reachable. | | **What version of the spec does the CLI use?** | It follows the **MapLibre Style Specification** bundled with the installed package. If you need to validate against a specific version (e.g., `v8` vs `v9`), install that version of `@maplibre/maplibre-style-spec` (`npm i @maplibre/maplibre-style-spec@8`). | | **My style uses custom extensions (`metadata.myApp:*`). Will the validator complain?** | No. The validator ignores unknown keys under `metadata`. Only top‑level keys that are not part of the spec will raise a warning. | | **I’m using a custom layer type (e.g., `type: "custom"`).** | The validator treats `custom` as a valid layer type, but you must ensure the runtime implementation (e.g., a custom WebGL layer) is loaded in your MapLibre app. | | **Can I validate multiple styles at once?** | Yes – just pass a glob pattern or loop over files in a script. The CLI accepts a single file path, so a simple Bash loop works: `for f in styles/*.json; do gl-style-validate "$f"; done`. | | **Is there a Node‑API (programmatic) version?** | Absolutely. You can import the validator in a script: ```js const { validate } = require('@maplibre/maplibre-style-spec'); const result = validate(styleObj); console.log(result.errors, result.warnings); ``` This is handy for custom build tools. | --- ## 9. TL;DR cheat‑sheet ```bash # Install once npm i -g @maplibre/maplibre-style-spec # Validate gl-style-validate -v path/to/style.json # Fix: # • Replace any mapbox:// URLs with HTTP(S) endpoints # • Add `sprite` and `glyphs` URLs that are reachable # • Convert `fog` → `sky` (or remove) # • Remove or rename `metadata.mapbox:*` keys (optional) # Re‑run until you see: # ✅ style is valid (0 errors, optional warnings) ``` Once the validator reports **zero errors**, you can safely load the style with MapLibre GL JS: ```javascript import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; import 'maplibre-gl/dist/maplibre-gl.css'; const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: '/styles/style.json', // <-- validated JSON center: [-122.42, 37.78], zoom: 12 }); ``` Happy mapping! 🎉 If you hit a specific error you can paste the message here and I’ll help you resolve it.

Below is a quick‑start guide that lets you **swap the `mapbox://…` style for a free, no‑key tile service** and see your map working in MapLibre right away. --- ## 1️⃣ Pick a “no‑API‑key” style to point the map at | Service | What it gives you | URL you can drop straight into `new maplibregl.Map({style: …})` | Notes | |---------|-------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|-------| | **MapLibre demo style** (the official “Hello World” style) | Vector tiles + sprites + glyphs hosted by the MapLibre team | `https://demotiles.maplibre.org/style.json` | Perfect for a first‑run test – it uses OpenStreetMap‑derived vector tiles and works everywhere. | | **OpenFreeMap** (community‑funded, no key) | Vector tiles, sprites, glyphs for the “Liberty” style | `https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/liberty` | Good if you want a more “Mapbox‑like” look. | | **OpenStreetMap raster tiles** (classic PNG tiles) | Raster tiles only (no vector style) | You create a style that points at `https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | Use this if you just need a simple basemap and don’t care about vector styling. | | **MapTiler Free style** (requires a key for higher‑quota plans, but works without one for low‑traffic testing) | Vector tiles from the OpenMapTiles schema | `https://api.maptiler.com/maps/streets/style.json?key=YOUR_KEY` → replace `YOUR_KEY` with an empty string for a “no‑key” test (the server will still serve a few tiles before throttling) | Good for a more polished look; you can sign up for a free key if you need more than a few hundred tiles. | > **TL;DR** – For a zero‑configuration sanity check, just use the MapLibre demo style: ```js style: 'https://demotiles.maplibre.org/style.json' ``` --- ## 2️⃣ Minimal MapLibre code that works with the demo style ```html MapLibre test – no token needed
``` Open the file in a browser (or serve it with `npx serve .`) and you should see a fully‑styled map **without any access token**. --- ## 3️⃣ If you need a custom style (e.g. you already have a Mapbox‑Studio JSON) 1. **Export the style JSON** from Mapbox Studio (File → Export → “Download style JSON”). 2. **Replace every `source` that uses `mapbox://`** with a URL that points at your new tile service. *For the demo style the source looks like this:* ```json "sources": { "openmaptiles": { "type": "vector", "url": "https://demotiles.maplibre.org/tiles/tiles.json" } } ``` 3. **Update sprite & glyph URLs** (they are also hosted on `mapbox://` by default). Example for the demo style: ```json "sprite": "https://demotiles.maplibre.org/sprite", "glyphs": "https://demotiles.maplibre.org/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf" ``` 4. **Save the edited JSON** somewhere you can fetch it (e.g. `public/style.json` in your project or a gist). 5. Point the map at that file: ```js style: '/style.json' // or a full URL if you host it elsewhere ``` **Tip:** Use **Maputnik** (https://maputnik.github.io/) to open the JSON, edit the source URLs visually, and validate the style against the MapLibre spec. You can even host Maputnik locally (`npm i -g maputnik && maputnik`) and load your style for quick iteration. --- ## 4️⃣ Quick “raster‑only” fallback (no vector style needed) If you just want to prove the map works and don’t care about vector styling, you can create a tiny style that points at the classic OSM raster tiles: ```json { "version": 8, "sources": { "osm-raster": { "type": "raster", "tiles": ["https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png"], "tileSize": 256, "attribution": "© OpenStreetMap contributors" } }, "layers": [ { "id": "osm-basemap", "type": "raster", "source": "osm-raster" } ] } ``` Save this as `raster-style.json` and use it as the `style` URL. No sprites or glyphs are required. --- ## 5️⃣ Checklist – “I’ve swapped the token, now what?” | ✅ | Action | |---|--------| | **1** | Install **maplibre-gl** (`npm i maplibre-gl`) and remove `mapbox-gl`. | | **2** | Change imports (`import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'`). | | **3** | Replace every `mapboxgl` reference with `maplibregl`. | | **4** | Delete `mapboxgl.accessToken = '…'`. | | **5** | **Set `style` to a non‑Mapbox URL** – use one of the free URLs above or a custom style you edited. | | **6** | If you use a custom style, verify that `sources`, `sprite`, and `glyphs` point at publicly reachable URLs (no `mapbox://`). | | **7** | Run the app – you should see the map load instantly. | | **8** | (Optional) Swap in a more production‑ready tile source later (self‑hosted PMTiles, OpenMapTiles, MapTiler Cloud, etc.). | --- ## 6️⃣ Where to go from here | Goal | Recommended next step | |------|-----------------------| | **Self‑host your own vector tiles** | Look at **Martin** (MapLibre’s tile server) or **PMTiles** + `maplibre-gl`’s `addSource({type:'vector',url:'pmtiles://…'})`. | | **Style editing** | Use **Maputnik** or **MapLibre Studio** (the open‑source fork of Mapbox Studio). | | **Add search / geocoding** | Swap Mapbox Geocoding for **Nominatim**, **Photon**, or a hosted service like **MapTiler Geocoding**. | | **Routing** | Replace Mapbox Directions with **OSRM**, **OpenRouteService**, or **Valhalla**. | | **Globe / 3‑D terrain** | Enable `terrain` and `sky` in the style (MapLibre v5+). | | **Performance testing** | Use the **MapLibre GL JS devtools** extension (Chrome) to inspect tile requests, GPU usage, etc. | --- ### TL;DR 1. **Pick a free style URL** – the easiest is `https://demotiles.maplibre.org/style.json`. 2. **Swap that URL into the `style` option** of your `new maplibregl.Map({ … })`. 3. **Remove the token** and you’re done – the map will load instantly with no API key. That gives you a working MapLibre map in seconds, and you can later replace the demo style with any custom style or self‑hosted tile source you prefer. Happy mapping! 🚀

Description: anti-pattern — assuming Mapbox v2 features work in MapLibre
prompt: I was using Mapbox GL JS v2 in my app, including map.setFog() and some v2-specific camera features. After migrating to MapLibre, these are broken. Did I do something wrong in the migration?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Thinking: We need to respond using the skill. Explain that map.setFog is not supported; need to use map.setSky and related style spec. Also camera features: MapLibre doesn't have FreeCameraOptions; need to use calculateCameraOptionsFromCameraLngLatAltRotation or other methods. Also note other migration steps. Provide guidance, code examples, checklist. Also mention that v2-specific APIs are not available; need to adapt. Provide resources. ## Short answer No – you didn’t miss a step. `map.setFog()` and the **Free‑camera** APIs that were added in Mapbox GL JS v2 simply **don’t exist in MapLibre**. MapLibre kept the v1.13 API surface (the one that existed before Mapbox went proprietary) and then added its own replacements: | Mapbox v2 feature | MapLibre equivalent (or “no direct equivalent”) | |-------------------|---------------------------------------------------| | `map.setFog({...})` (and the `fog` root‑level style object) | **`map.setSky({...})`** with a `sky` root‑level style object. The property names are different (e.g. `sky-color`, `horizon-color`, `fog-color`, `fog-ground-blend`, …). | | `map.getFreeCameraOptions()` / `map.setFreeCameraOptions()` (FreeCameraOptions class) | **No direct API**. Use the new camera‑calculation helpers (`calculateCameraOptionsFromCameraLngLatAltRotation`, `calculateCameraOptionsFromTo`, etc.) and then call `jumpTo`, `easeTo` or `flyTo`. | | `map.setFog`‑related methods (`setFog`, `getFog`) | Not present. Use the **sky** API instead. | | `map.setFreeCameraOptions`‑related methods | Not present. Use the **camera‑options** helpers described below. | So the migration is correct; you just need to replace those calls with the MapLibre‑specific ones. Below is a **complete “what to change” guide** for those two problem areas, plus a quick sanity‑check checklist to make sure the rest of your migration is solid. --- ## 1️⃣ Replace `map.setFog()` → `map.setSky()` ### Why it’s different * Mapbox introduced a **Fog** layer in v2 that lives under the `fog` top‑level style property. * MapLibre never added a `fog` object. Instead it introduced a **Sky** layer (experimental in v5, stable in v6) that can render both a sky gradient and fog‑like effects. ### How to translate a typical Fog config | Mapbox `setFog` example | MapLibre `setSky` equivalent | |--------------------------|------------------------------| | ```js
map.setFog({
"color": "#f8f4f0",
"high-color": "#245b8c",
"space-color": "#c8d0e0",
"horizon-blend": 0.3,
"star-intensity": 0.0
});``` | ```js
map.setSky({
"sky-color": "#245b8c", // replaces high‑color
"horizon-color": "#f8f4f0", // replaces color
"space-color": "#c8d0e0", // same name
"fog-color": "#f8f4f0", // optional – you can reuse the horizon color
"fog-ground-blend": 0.3, // similar to horizon‑blend
"horizon-fog-blend": 0.3,
"sky-horizon-blend": 0.3,
"atmosphere-blend": 1.0
});``` | #### Minimal working example ```javascript // MapLibre v6+ (ES‑module import shown) import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; import 'maplibre-gl/dist/maplibre-gl.css'; const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: 'https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/liberty', // any non‑Mapbox style center: [-122.42, 37.78], zoom: 12, pitch: 45, // pitch needed to see the sky bearing: 0 }); // Wait for the style to load before calling setSky map.on('style.load', () => { map.setSky({ 'sky-color': '#245b8c', 'horizon-color': '#f8f4f0', 'space-color': '#c8d0e0', 'fog-color': '#f8f4f0', 'fog-ground-blend': 0.3, 'horizon-fog-blend': 0.3, 'sky-horizon-blend': 0.3, 'atmosphere-blend': 1.0 }); }); ``` **Things to remember** * The `sky` object must be present in the *style JSON* (or you can add it at runtime with `setSky`). If you’re editing a style file manually, add a top‑level `"sky": {}` entry. * The sky only renders when the map has a non‑zero `pitch`. If you keep the map flat (`pitch: 0`), you’ll see a solid background colour instead. * The `sky` spec is still marked **experimental** (as of v6), so some properties may change in future releases. Keep an eye on the [MapLibre Style Spec – Sky](https://maplibre.org/maplibre-style-spec/sky/) page. --- ## 2️⃣ Replace Free‑Camera APIs ### What Mapbox gave you ```js // Mapbox v2 const cam = map.getFreeCameraOptions(); cam.position = [lng, lat, altitude]; cam.orientation = { pitch: 45, bearing: 30, roll: 0 }; map.setFreeCameraOptions(cam); ``` ### What MapLibre provides MapLibre’s camera model is still based on **center, zoom, pitch, bearing, and (since v3) elevation**. There is **no `FreeCameraOptions` class**. Instead you: 1. **Calculate a `CameraOptions` object** from the desired lng/lat/altitude and orientation using one of the helper methods. 2. **Pass that object** to `jumpTo`, `easeTo`, or `flyTo`. #### Helper methods (v5+) | Helper | What it does | Typical use | |--------|--------------|-------------| | `map.calculateCameraOptionsFromCameraLngLatAltRotation(lngLat, altitude, bearing, pitch, roll)` | Returns a full `CameraOptions` (center, zoom, pitch, bearing, roll, elevation) that matches the given “free‑camera” pose. | Direct replacement for a single `setFreeCameraOptions` call. | | `map.calculateCameraOptionsFromTo(fromLngLat, altitudeFrom, toLngLat, altitudeTo, bearing, pitch, roll)` | Returns a `CameraOptions` that looks from `from` to `to` (a “look‑at” camera). | Useful for “fly from A to B” scenarios. | | `map.calculateCameraOptionsFromBounds(bounds, options?)` | Returns a `CameraOptions` that fits the given bounds (similar to `fitBounds`). | Already existed in Mapbox, still works. | #### Example conversion ```javascript // Mapbox v2 – free camera const freeCam = map.getFreeCameraOptions(); freeCam.position = [-122.42, 37.78, 500]; // lng, lat, altitude (meters) freeCam.orientation = { pitch: 45, bearing: 30, roll: 0 }; map.setFreeCameraOptions(freeCam); ``` ```javascript // MapLibre v6 – equivalent // 1️⃣ Compute the CameraOptions const camOpts = map.calculateCameraOptionsFromCameraLngLatAltRotation( [-122.42, 37.78], // lngLat 500, // altitude in meters 30, // bearing 45, // pitch 0 // roll (optional, default 0) ); // 2️⃣ Apply it – choose the transition you want map.jumpTo(camOpts); // instant // or map.easeTo(camOpts, {duration: 2000}); // smooth // or map.flyTo(camOpts, {speed: 1.2}); // “fly” animation ``` **Key points** * `altitude` → **elevation** (MapLibre’s `CameraOptions` property).
